body.objective: Students will be able to analyze music's role in social movements.
body.iCan: I can analyze music's role in social movements.
successCriteria: I can explain how music has supported social movements
I can analyze lyrics and musical choices in a protest song
I can describe how music still connects to activism today
body.hook: In 1963, 250,000 people at the March on Washington heard Mahalia Jackson and Bob Dylan sing. In 1969, John Lennon and Yoko Ono recorded "Give Peace a Chance" in a hotel bed in Montreal. Music has been the soundtrack of nearly every movement for change.

vocabulary.definition: A song written to support a cause or criticize injustice.
A group effort by many people to bring about social change.
A song adopted by a group to express shared identity or purpose.
A pattern where a leader sings and a group answers.
CRTC rules requiring Canadian radio to play a share of Canadian music.

study.title: Songs That Changed Things
study.question: How has music helped people push for social change?
study.passage:
Examples (teachers choose recordings and check lyrics for classroom use):
• "We Shall Overcome": an adapted gospel hymn that became the anthem of the US civil rights movement in the 1960s. Simple, repetitive, easy for crowds to sing together.
• "Give Peace a Chance" (1969): recorded by John Lennon and Yoko Ono in Montreal, sung at anti-Vietnam War rallies.
• Buffy Sainte-Marie (Cree), "Universal Soldier" (1964): an anti-war song questioning individual responsibility.
• "Biko" by Peter Gabriel (1980): about South African anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko.
• A Tribe Called Red (now The Halluci Nation): combines powwow drums and electronic music to celebrate Indigenous identity.
Musical tools of protest: singable melodies and repetition, call and response, borrowing familiar tunes, powerful lyrics, crowd participation.
Task: In groups, analyze one song: context, message, lyric techniques (repetition, imagery, direct address), musical choices and impact. Present a three-minute analysis.
study.source: Case study written for this lesson; summarized from music history sources.

Can a song actually change laws or opinions?

examples.title: Singability
examples.problem: Why does "We Shall Overcome" work for marches?
examples.answer: Slow tempo, simple stepwise melody and repeated lines let crowds sing together
examples.explore: What would make a song hard to march with?

examples.title: Lyric technique
examples.problem: What does repetition do in a protest chorus?
examples.answer: It makes the message memorable and lets everyone join in

examples.title: Borrowing
examples.problem: Why adapt existing hymns or folk tunes?
examples.answer: People already know the tune, so they can sing new words immediately

examples.title: CanCon
examples.answer: A requirement that Canadian radio play a percentage of Canadian music
examples.explore: How does it help Canadian artists?
